title: Sales enablement: positioning, competitive briefs, pitch deck guidance, pricing & security FAQ
author: Ava Martinez
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook provides a single-page reference for Redwood Inference sales and pre-sales teams to articulate positioning and messaging, run competitive conversations, assemble a prospect pitch deck, provide pricing guidance, show concise case studies, and answer common security questions for prospects. Intended audience: AEs, SEs, SDRs, partner sellers, and GTM enablement content authors.

Use guidance: Keep short-form messaging for discovery calls, use the competitive brief for objection handling and battle cards, and assemble the recommended pitch deck outline for demos and executive presentations. Update cadence: quarterly or when product/pricing changes materially.

1) Executive positioning and core messaging

- Problem statement:
  - Modern product teams need predictable, cost-effective inference for LLM-powered features but face rising token costs, brittle latency, and operational complexity across hosted, dedicated, and private environments.
- Redwood thesis (one-liner):
  - "Redwood Inference provides a unified runtime and developer experience that makes LLM inference predictable, economical, and reliable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments."
- Three core messages (talking points):
  1. Production-first performance: low P99 latency and high throughput with GPU-optimized serving and intelligent batching (proof: internal perf profiles, typical P95 latency for 512-token workloads on hosted = 180-300 ms; Dedicated capacity offers SLA-backed throughput).
  2. Deployment flexibility and governance: same API and rollout controls across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private so customers can evolve from self-serve to enterprise-grade without rewrites (proof: VPC private control plane, KMS integrations, audit logs).
  3. Cost-aware controls: actionable levers (quantization profiles, autoscaling/burst policies, prefix caching) that produce measurable unit-cost reductions without sacrificing quality (proof: Optimize suggestions that typically reduce per-token cost 20-45% on benchmarked workloads).
- Elevator pitch (10-20s):
  - "Redwood Inference gives engineering teams predictable, low-latency LLM inference across hosted, reserved, and private deployments — so you can ship features fast while controlling cost, compliance, and uptime."
- 30s/2min pitch scripts: provided in the SE playbook snippets folder (link in related_pages).

2) Competitive brief (quick reference)

Format: competitor -> recommended framing -> strengths -> weaknesses -> close patterns / battle card bullets.

- Competitor: Major cloud AI endpoints (CloudX AI, BigCloud LLM endpoints)
  - Framing: Customers choose managed endpoints for convenience, but often trade off predictable latency, cost transparency, and model portability.
  - Strengths: Deep cloud integrations, broad regional coverage, simple procurement for cloud-native teams.
  - Weaknesses: Higher variable cost for sustained throughput; limited private deployment options; vendor lock-in to specific infra.
  - Close pattern: Emphasize Redwood Dedicated/reserved options for predictable monthly costs and our migration playbook for lifting workloads off the public endpoint without code changes.

- Competitor: LLM API providers (ProviderA, ProviderB)
  - Framing: API-first providers emphasize simplicity and curated models.
  - Strengths: Polished SDKs, generous free tiers, quick prototyping.
  - Weaknesses: Less operational transparency and fewer enterprise deployment controls; limited options for on-prem or strict data residency.
  - Close pattern: Stress Redwood’s observability (token-level cost, per-model dashboards) and Private offering for regulated customers.

- Competitor: Inference infra vendors / self-hosted runtimes (OpenInference, Custom on-prem stacks)
  - Framing: Self-hosted gives full control but requires hiring ops expertise and continuous tuning.
  - Strengths: Full ownership, potential cost savings at extremely large scale.
  - Weaknesses: Significant engineering overhead (serving runtime, kernel selection, batching, KV cache), long lead time to production, and no commercial SLA.
  - Close pattern: Position Redwood as a middle ground — we provide a production-grade runtime plus operations expertise and a predictable cost model. Offer a migration plan and TCO comparison.

- Quick battle-card bullets (use during objection handling):
  - "We can guarantee predictable latency/throughput via Dedicated and region routing — ask about your 99th percentile latency SLOs and we’ll show a capacity plan."
  - "If data residency or compliance is a blocker, our Private offering supports VPC and on-prem deployments with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs."
  - "We instrument token-level cost and can produce a 3-month cost forecast showing expected per-feature spend and savings from caching/quantization."

3) Pitch deck outline (slide-by-slide)

Recommended slide sequence (include notes for visuals and metrics):
1. Title / Team (1 slide) — short tagline, logo, presenter’s name, and ask.
2. Problem (1 slide) — bullets describing customer pain (latency spikes, unpredictable costs, compliance headaches). Visual: annotated architecture of current pain points.
3. Opportunity / Market (1 slide) — developer adoption, growth of LLM features, typical ARR impact of LLM features.
4. Redwood solution (1-2 slides) — short architecture diagram showing Hosted, Dedicated, Private, and unified API. Visual callouts: caching, batching, routing.
5. Differentiators (1 slide) — production-first runtime, rollout controls, cost tooling, private deployments. Include 3-4 quick proof points.
6. Demo / Live example (1-2 slides) — show a real-time console screenshot or short recorded clip of streaming generation + cost pane and per-model latency dashboard.
7. Performance & SLOs (1 slide) — sample P95/P99 numbers, throughput, and Dedicated SLA terms.
8. Pricing & Commercials (1 slide) — high-level pricing bands and engagement models (see pricing guidance).
9. Security & Compliance (1 slide) — bullet list of certifications, encryption in transit/at rest, audit logging, and private deployment options.
10. Case studies / customer proof (1-2 slides) — short bullets with metrics (see case studies).
11. Implementation plan & timeline (1 slide) — phases (POC, pilot, rollout), typical timeline (2-8 weeks depending on scope).
12. Ask & next steps (1 slide) — trial access, pilot terms, SE contact.

Slide notes: bring an SE to technical reviews; include a TCO appendix showing per-token model cost breakdown and example quantization impact. Keep the main deck to 12 slides.

4) Pricing guidance (sales-friendly summary)

High-level models: Hosted (usage-based), Dedicated (reserved capacity with commit + overage), Private (license + support + optional managed services). Use the following negotiation levers: term length, committed throughput, model selection (open vs proprietary), observability retention, and professional services for integration.

Example bands (reference only — check pricing sheet before quoting):
- Hosted API (self-serve / paid):
  - Developer tier: free credits then pay-as-you-go (retail).
  - Production: volume tiers with per-token pricing and per-embedding unit pricing. Typical ranges: $0.0003–$0.003 per input token equivalent depending on model and volume.
- Dedicated (monthly commit):
  - Small pool: predictable baseline throughput for SMB / high-growth startups (starts ~$10k/mo committed).
  - Mid/Enterprise pools: negotiated based on GPU type, throughput, and regional needs; includes SLA and private routing.
- Private (VPC / on-prem):
  - Platform license + deployment fee + support tier. Pricing varies by scale and compliance needs; commonly mid-six-figure ARR for large global deployments.

Discount guidance and negotiation tips:
- Offer onboarding credits for pilots and a fixed 60-90 day pilot evaluation window.
- Use committed throughput and multi-year terms as primary discount levers (12-24 month commitments commonly reduce 10-25%).
- Bundle observability retention or professional services for migration as valued add-ons rather than reducing base price.
- For price-sensitive prospects, emphasize Optimize (quantization and caching) to reduce effective per-token cost and offer a structured ROI study.

Contractual items to surface early: data processing addenda, SOC2/ISO evidence, KMS/HSM key management, and support SLAs for Dedicated. Loop legal early for enterprise buys.

5) Case studies (short, sales-friendly 1-paragraph synopses + metrics)

- Case study: SearchStart (SaaS startup) — problem: slow query latency and high per-query cost after moving to LLM reranking.
  - Solution: Migrated to Redwood Dedicated with prefix caching and model quantization.
  - Outcome: 40% reduction in per-query token cost, P95 latency reduced from 760ms to 220ms, and 18% increase in user engagement on search results.
  - Quote: "Redwood gave us predictable latency and a clear path to scale without re-architecting our stack." — VP Eng, SearchStart.

- Case study: FinServe Inc. (regulated enterprise) — problem: compliance and data residency blocked public-hosted endpoints.
  - Solution: Private deployment with VPC control plane, HSM-backed key management, and audit log integration with the customer's SIEM.
  - Outcome: Passed vendor security review, met in-region data residency requirements, and shortened procurement cycle by using Redwood's prescriptive security questionnaire.
  - Quote: "The Private deployment met our compliance bar with minimal ops burden." — Head of Information Security, FinServe Inc.

Appendix: contact for full case studies and slide-ready one-pagers: go-to-market case studies library (link in related_pages).

6) Security FAQ for prospects (concise answers for first-level prospect questions)

Q1: Where does customer data reside?
A: Hosted customers choose region(s) for deployment; Dedicated customers get tenant-isolated GPU pools in specified regions; Private supports VPC, on-prem and in-region deployments. We provide clear data residency statements in the contract and can map to customer expectations during procurement.

Q2: How is data encrypted?
A: Encryption in transit is TLS 1.2/1.3. At rest encryption with AES-256; for Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM.

Q3: Do you retain prompts, responses, or logs?
A: Default retention windows are configurable; for Hosted we retain logs for observability and billing; Dedicated/Private customers can opt for reduced retention or no-retention policies per contract. All retention policies are documented in the DPA.

Q4: What certifications do you hold?
A: Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II and is working toward ISO 27001 (status page in security-and-compliance). For enterprise deals we provide a redacted SOC 2 report and a standardized security questionnaire.

Q5: How is access controlled?
A: Role-based access control (RBAC) in the Console, API keys with scoped permissions, and audit logs for administrative actions. Private deployments can integrate with customer SSO (SAML/OIDC).

Q6: How are incidents handled and communicated?
A: We maintain an incident response playbook, customer notification policy and a status page. For Dedicated and Private customers we provide a runbook with escalation contacts and an operational cadence.

Q7: Can we run models on-prem or air-gapped?
A: Yes — Private on-prem packaging supports air-gapped deployments with optional managed services. Work with Solutions Engineering to scope networking and hardware.

Q8: How do you support key management?
A: We integrate with major KMS providers (Cloud KMS, AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault) and support HSM-backed customer-managed keys for Private deployments.

Q9: Will Redwood train or fine-tune models on customer data?
A: Redwood does not perform model training on customer data as part of hosted inference. For specialized professional services engagements, training/fine-tuning is scoped, contracted, and governed by a separate DPA and security assessment.

Technical appendix (short examples and references)

- Sample audit evidence package: SOC 2 Type II report, penetration test summary, data flow diagram, and redacted config screenshots.
- SE tip: Ask the prospect what their procurement security checklist requires (e.g., encryption at rest, pen test, SOC 2). If they ask for timeframe, typical readiness for Private deployment + security review is 4-8 weeks depending on contract.

7) Handling common sales objections (concise rebuttals)

- "Your price is too high" -> "Let's run a 3-month cost forecast. Many customers find cost drops after enabling caching/quantization and we can show the expected ROI; alternatively, consider a Dedicated commit to reduce unit cost."
- "We already use CloudX endpoints" -> "If you need a migration, we provide a migration playbook and can run a small pilot to validate parity and measure latency/cost improvements."
- "We need air-gapped on-prem" -> "We support on-prem Private packaging and will engage Solutions Engineering to create a deployment and SOW."

8) Operational checklist for pilots (step-by-step)

1. Discovery: capture traffic profile, typical prompt sizes, compliance requirements, and deployment preference (Hosted/Dedicated/Private).
2. Proposal: produce cost forecast and recommended model/quantization profiles.
3. Pilot setup: create trial account or Dedicated small pool; enable observability dashboards and link billing.
4. Validate metrics: measure P95/P99 latency, token unit cost, and quality regression with the customer's evaluation prompts.
5. Pilot review: present results, propose production plan, and negotiate commercial terms.

Estimated timeline: 2-8 weeks. Ownership: AE (commercial), SE (technical), Solutions Eng (Private feasibility), Legal (DPA).
